[MATH: r|= (a_{2})/(a_{1}) = (12)/(4) = 3]

[MATH: S_N = \dfrac{a_1 (1-r^N) }{1-r}.]

Now, we rewrite [MATH: 243] as [MATH: 3^{5},] which gives

Content:
Finally, since both sides of the equation share the same base [MATH: (3),] we equate the exponents:

Content:

Content:
The sum of the first [MATH: N] terms of a geometric series can be determined by the formula

Substituting [MATH: a_1= 2] and [MATH: r =2,] we get the following:

[MATH: S_{N}|= (2(1 − 2^{N}))/(1 − 2); = 2(2^{N} − 1)]

Content:
If this is to exceed [MATH: 620,] then the following must be true:

Content:
[MATH: 2(2^{N} − 1)|> 620; 2^{N} − 1|> 310; 2^{N}|> 311]

Content:
Now, we take [MATH: \log] of both sides of the equation and use the power rule to solve for [MATH: N,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \log (2^{N})|> \log (311); N\log 2|> \log (311); N|> (\log (311))/(\log 2); N|> 8.281…]

Content:
Since [MATH: N] must be an integer, we conclude that there need to be at least [MATH: 9] terms for the given sum to exceed [MATH: 620.]

The sum of the first [MATH: N] terms of a geometric series can be determined by the formula

[MATH: S_N = \dfrac{a_1 (1-r^N) }{1-r}.]

Substituting [MATH: a_1= 1] and [MATH: r =4,] we get the following:

[MATH: S_{N}|= 1 ⋅ (1 − 4^{N})/(1 − 4); = (4^{N} − 1)/(3)]

If this is to exceed [MATH: 240,] then the following must be true:

[MATH: (4^{N} − 1)/(3)|> 240; 4^{N} − 1|> 720; 4^{N}|> 721]

Now, we take [MATH: \log] of both sides of the equation and use the power rule to solve for [MATH: N,] as follows:

[MATH: \log (4^{N})|> \log (721); N\log 4|> \log (721); N|> (\log (721))/(\log 4); N|> 4.746…]

Since [MATH: N] must be an integer, we conclude that there need to be at least [MATH: 5] terms for the given sum to exceed [MATH: 240.]

[MATH: S_{N}|= 2 ⋅ (1 − 2^{N})/(1 − 2); = 2 ⋅ (1 − 2^{N})/(− 1); = 2(2^{N} − 1)]

If this is to not exceed [MATH: 1\,000,] then the following must be true:

In this case, [MATH: a_1= 4] and [MATH: r = 3.] Substituting our values into the above formula, we get the following:

Now, we rewrite [MATH: 243] as [MATH: 3^{5},] which gives

Content:
[MATH: 3^{N}|= 3^{5}.]

Content:
Finally, since both sides of the equation share the same base [MATH: (3),] we equate the exponents:

Content:
[MATH: N|= 5]
